title: Lahore, 1765
hook: Sikh chiefs entered Lahore and struck coins in the Gurus' names

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thirty at the Harmandir, who stayed when staying meant dying. Your line was thirty stood. Which small duty did you stay with? Today, a city and a coin. Day eight hundred seventy.

Check the coins in a pocket or a purse. Whose face is on them? Whose name? A coin goes where no army goes: into markets, kitchens, and strangers' hands. So when Sikh chiefs rode into Lahore, the great city where Sikhs had been hunted, tortured and killed, there was an obvious next step, the thing anyone holding a city does. Strike a coin. The question is whose name to put on it. Today: Lahore.
screen: `A COIN TRAVELS FARTHER THAN AN ARMY.` → `SIKH CHIEFS RIDE INTO LAHORE.` → `WHOSE NAME GOES ON THE COIN?`

segments.voice: First, the city. Lahore was the seat of governors this path has met in the hard years, with its prisons and its executions. Now Sikh chiefs held it. Second, the coin. Tradition says the coins they struck carried no chief's name. Instead they carried a short verse in Persian, the language of coins and courts, naming Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. In the common telling, the verse says that the deg, the teg and the fateh, along with the help that came without delay, were received from Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. Third, the three words, because they're worth slowing down for. Deg is a big cooking pot, the kind used in the langar, the free kitchen. Teg is a sword. Fateh is victory. So the pot comes before the sword. Feeding people is named first, defending them second, and the victory is credited to the Gurus. A chief could have stamped his own name and claimed the win. Here, the coin says it wasn't theirs to claim. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. Whatever we put our name on tells people what we think we own. Sikhs remember this coin as one that pointed past the people who made it. The gurus' coin.
screen: `LAHORE: THE CITY OF THE HARD YEARS.` · `NO CHIEF'S NAME, THE GURUS' NAMES.` · `DEG, TEG, FATEH: POT, SWORD, VICTORY.` · `THE CREDIT GOES PAST THE CHIEFS.` · then, large: `THE GURUS' COIN.`

segments.voice: For this sit, find something minted. A coin is perfect; a medal, a stamped key or a banknote works too. Hold it in your palm. Feel its weight. Look at what's on it: a face, a name, a building, a motto. Someone decided that. Breathe slowly, and ask what you'd want stamped on your own work, if anything. Whose name would it carry? Let the question sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Lahore. Tradition says that when Sikh chiefs took the city, they struck coins carrying not their own names but the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. Today's word.
Your line: the gurus' coin. Today, when something you did goes well, name one person or one gift that made it possible, before you take the credit. Day eight hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Coins struck by Sikh rulers in the Gurus' names are kept in museums and collections, and Sikhs still use the phrase deg teg fateh for the ideals of feeding and protecting.

original.note: Gurmukhi for deg teg fateh: the cooking pot, the sword, and victory.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Sikhs took Lahore and made money in their own name.
what it means: tradition says the coins named the Gurus, with the words deg, teg and fateh.
what a scholar hears: the Persian verse credits the pot, the sword and victory to Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, a coin pointing past its makers.

notes: The coin's Persian couplet ('Degh o tegh o fateh o nusrat bedirang / yaft az Nanak Guru Gobind Singh') is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the paraphrase and that it appeared on the coins struck at Lahore in this period.
The chiefs at Lahore are not named (commonly Lehna Singh, Gujjar Singh and Sobha Singh); confirm whether to name them.
'Lahore is where much of the hard century's suffering was ordered and carried out' is a general claim; soften if needed.
Gurmukhi ਦੇਗ ਤੇਗ ਫ਼ਤਿਹ and pronunciation; confirm.
No year is given in the voice; the index title has 1765.
Editor: merged two back-to-back 'this path has' sentences.
Audit: removed 'no chief's face' (coins of the region did not normally carry portraits, so it implied a choice that wasn't one); teach, screen and myth now speak of names only.
